extracted.intended_audience: mathematics-education researchers, teacher-educators, and graduate students studying mathematical connections and classroom argumentation
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of mathematical connections in proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and methodological guidance for identifying and analyzing mathematical connections and argumentation in classroom proofs, by networking the Extended Theory of Connections (ETC) with the Theory of Mathematical Argumentation (TMA) using Toulmin's model and thematic analysis of classroom episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of mathematical connection (ETC)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical connection is understood as “a cognitive process through which a person relates two or more ideas, concepts, definitions, theorems, procedures, representations, and meanings with each other, with other disciplines or with real life” (García-García & Dolores-Flores, 2018, p.229).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this working definition to identify instances where a subject relates concepts/representations/meanings; connections may be intra- or extra-mathematical. The paper treats connections as a process that can be detected in written productions, oral or mimicked arguments, and as having a supporting correspondence code between objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural: evident when rules, algorithms or formulas are used to arrive at a result (García-García, 2019; García-García & Dolores-Flores, 2019).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: using the slope formula m = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1) to find the line's slope. Identify uses of procedures/algorithms as evidence of procedural connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Part–whole connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Part-whole: occurs when someone identifies that A is a generalization of B, where B is a particular case of A (Businskas, 2008).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: recognizing P(x)=x^3 - x^2 - 9x -9 as a particular case of f(x)=ax^3+bx^2+cx+d. Look for inclusion/generalization relationships or identification of a concept as a special case of a more general one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Implication: based on a logical if-then relationship (A→B) (Businskas, 2008).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example explicitly given: ‘if f is differentiable at x=a, then f is continuous at x=a.’ Identify explicit logical implication relations used as connections in arguments or proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different-representations connection (alternate/equivalent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different representations: can be alternate (representing a concept in two or more different registers, e.g., graph–algebraic, verbal–graph) or equivalent (transformations within the same register, e.g., algebraic–algebraic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: P(x) graphed (graphical) vs P(x) factored (symbolic). Distinguish alternate (different semiotic registers) from equivalent (same register, transformed) representations when coding connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature: identified when the subject manifests characteristics or properties of concepts, describing similarities or differences to others (Eli et al., 2011; García-García & Dolores-Flores, 2019).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: naming coefficients, variables, exponents of a polynomial. Code mentions of properties/elements that locate a concept among others as feature-connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaning: presented when students attribute a meaning to a mathematical concept (what it is for them, what it represents), possibly including their constructed definition (García-García, 2019, p.131).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ‘the derivative f′(a) is the instantaneous rate of change.’ Capture statements that link concept to meaning or use-context as meaning connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversibility connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversibility: present when a subject starts from concept A to get to B and can invert the process starting from B to return to A (García-García & Dolores-Flores, 2019).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: recognizing the bidirectional relationship between derivative and integral via the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Look for bidirectional reasoning or operators viewed as inverses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphorical connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphorical: projection of properties/characteristics of a known domain to structure another less-known domain (Rodríguez-Nieto et al., 2022a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: verbal expressions like “travel through the graph without lifting the pencil,” implying the conceptual metaphor 'the graph is a path.' Identify metaphors that structure conceptual understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic scheme of mathematical connection (correspondence code)
rubrics_metrics.description: Connections schematized as two mathematical objects that are connected and supported by a correspondence code (Rodríguez-Nieto et al., 2021b, 2022b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should seek the two objects and the correspondence code that supports the linkage (e.g., derivative at a point ↔ slope of tangent line, supported by the meaning/correspondence). Use this scheme to structure coding of connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification criterion for connections in student productions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical connections emerge when students solve specific tasks and can identify them in their written productions or in the oral or mimic arguments they develop (García-García & Dolores-Flores, 2018, p.229).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing data, treat explicit references in written/oral/mimed work as evidence of connection; design tasks to elicit such productions for reliable identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of semi-structured/task-based interviews and thematic analysis to identify connections
rubrics_metrics.description: ETC-informed research often applies semi-structured interviews or task-based interviews to collect data and uses thematic/content analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006) to identify phrases/keywords from which connection types are inferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological recommendation: collect verbal/written data via tasks/interviews and code units of meaning; infer connection types from coded phrases and topics using thematic analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toulmin's basic argument structure (TMA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic structure consists of Data (D), Conclusion (C), and Warrant (W). Backing (B), Modal qualifier (Q), and Refutations/Rebuttals (R) exist but were not considered in this study (Toulmin, 1984/2003).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reconstruct classroom utterances by mapping utterances to D, W, C; use the model to expose how mathematical properties (warrants) justify the link between data and conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the warrant in mathematical proof/argumentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The warrant supports the conclusion based on mathematical theorems, axioms, definitions or properties, and provides an idea about the type of reasoning adopted by the arguer (Pedemonte & Balacheff, 2016; Cervantes-Barraza et al., 2020, 2022).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing proofs/arguments, pay special attention to warrants as loci where mathematical connections appear; classify the warrant content to infer the underlying connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of warrants (classification used in teacher argumentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers' warrants can involve categories such as: (1) use of theorems or mathematical properties (a priori), (2) reliance on mathematics textbook content, (3) appeals to what has been consolidated in the class (institutional/class consensus), and (4) pedagogical/valuative justifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code warrants by these content-types to capture epistemic, institutional and pedagogical bases of teacher argumentation; recognize that non-mathematical warrants (pedagogical, evaluative) influence argumentation analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of proof (Stylianides)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is a mathematical argument that: (1) uses statements accepted by the classroom community (true and available without further justification), (2) employs modes of reasoning that are valid and within the classroom community's conceptual reach, and (3) is communicated with forms of expression appropriate and known to that community (Stylianides, 2007).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate classroom proofs against these three criteria to distinguish rigorous proofs from everyday argumentation; consider community acceptance and communicative modes in classroom contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of mathematical arguments (Toulmin/Godden & Walton)
rubrics_metrics.description: Toulmin’s and related taxonomies list argument types based on reasoning: analogy, rule, effect, generalization, sign, cause, authority, classification, etc. (Toulmin, 2003; Godden & Walton, 2007).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these typologies to categorize argumentative patterns in classroom discourse and to relate warrant-content to argument form (e.g., analogical vs. classificatory arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective-argumentation types (Cervantes-Barraza adaptation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Five adapted argument types for collective argumentation: Argument from classification; Argument from mathematical properties; Practical argument; Argument from best explanation; Argument from consequences (Cervantes-Barraza, 2020).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In group/class discourse, classify arguments by their warrant/content emphasis (classification, properties, practical comparison, best-explanation, consequences) to understand how collective reasoning is structured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for typifying arguments in classroom research
rubrics_metrics.description: Typifications can be based on integration of mathematical reasoning elements (case, rule, result) and basic argument elements (data, warrant, conclusion) — e.g., Conner et al. (2014) — or on objects/processes/mathematical statements as Molina et al. (2019) for abductive/analogy arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When labeling argument types, consider both formal logical structure and the mathematical objects/processes invoked; multiple typification schemes may be combined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality assessment of mathematical connections (representation emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research tools (e.g., Mhlolo, 2012) analyze the nature and quality of mathematical connections with emphasis on representations and higher cognitive levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply validated instruments or task-based rubrics to assess connection quality (e.g., depth, multiplicity of registers, integration of meaning and procedure); focus on representational richness as an indicator of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Networking-of-theories strategies (Prediger et al.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four pairs of sub-strategies to articulate theories ranging from ignoring another framework to global unification: (1) compression/hierarchical ordering by experts, (2) comparison and contrast to find commonalities/differences, (3) combination and coordination to generate conceptual complementarities, and (4) local integration/synthesis to form holistic frameworks (Prediger et al., 2008).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When combining ETC and TMA, follow these strategies sequentially: understand each theory, compare/contrast, coordinate/ combine tools for joint analysis, and seek local synthesis; explicitly justify chosen networking strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory components to respect when networking (Radford's P–M–Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory comprises: P (system of basic principles delimiting the universe of discourse), M (methodology including data-collection & interpretation techniques), and Q (paradigmatic research questions/templates) — these components must be connected when networking theories (Radford, 2008).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In networking theories, ensure alignment and explicit treatment of each theory's principles, methods, and paradigmatic questions; document how P, M and Q are coordinated to avoid conceptual or methodological mismatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological design for studying teacher proof episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative design recommended: use non-participant video-recorded classroom observation of teacher proof enactments, collect episodes, and analyze arguments via Toulmin model reconstruction plus thematic analysis to identify mathematical connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps: recruit voluntary teacher participant(s), videotape proof sessions, segment episodes, reconstruct argument elements (D,W,C), code for connection types using ETC categories, and perform thematic coding to infer patterns and complementarities between theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research question templates for ETC vs TMA comparative work
rubrics_metrics.description: Sample research questions guiding ETC research: Which connections are promoted? What is the quality level of connections? What factors generate typologies? For TMA: What are characteristics of complex argumentation? How do students develop argumentation? (Examples of Q-templates used)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these paradigmatic question templates to shape investigations that seek complementarities between connection-analysis and argumentation-analysis; align data collection instruments to answer these templates (tasks, interviews, classroom recordings).
